newsitem.title: USA: US sees improved copyright enforcement by China.
newsitem.headline: US sees improved copyright enforcement by China.

text.p: The United States on Friday said there were indications that China was doing a better job at enforcing a U.S.-China accord to prevent piracy of U.S. compact discs (CDs), particularly in Guangdong Province.

Acting U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky said a team of U.S. trade officials in Guangdong this week reported that four underground CD factories and nine CD production lines had been shut down in recent weeks.
In addition, Chinese customs authorities had stepped up their efforts at the border, targeting the illegal import of CD production equipment, Barshefsky said in a statement.
At the same time, U.S. imports of audiovisual products, especially sound recordings and motion pictures, had increased somewhat over last year's levels, she said.
U.S. trade officials acknowledged progress by China in implementing the U.S.-China accord, but said they were continuing to the Chinese efforts.
Additionally, the United States completed an "out-of-cycle" review of efforts by Greece, Russia, Saudi Arabia, Argentina, the Philippines and Hong Kong to protect copyrights and patents.
Barshefsky said piracy of U.S. motion pictures remained a large problem in Greece, where films are routinely broadcast on Greek TV without payment of royalties.
She said Greece remained on the so-called "priority watch list", although Greece had developed and presented a plan of specific steps to address the problem.

Barshefsky termed the Greek plan "a step in the right direction," and said she would look forward to its implementation by next April, the time of the next regular U.S. review of copyright and patent protection.

Barshefsky said Russia was also continuing to take steps to address U.S. concerns, including passage of a new law to increase criminal penalties and major enforcement actions, but piracy of U.S. products remained a big problem.
Saudi Arabia was continuing to make progress, albeit at a very slow pace, Barshefsky said, resulting in her decision to keep it on the "watch list."
Argentina remained on the "priority watch list", pending a U.S. review of a new law regarding the protection of exclusive test data.
Washington was also reviewing the status of the Philippines, now on the "watch list".
Hong Kong was not added to the list, Barshefsky said, but she cited ongoing concerns about Hong Kong's efforts to prevent the reverse engineering of proprietary software, or software decompilation.
